doctitle: ELPS Supports — Critical Thinking Online Breakouts
h1: ELPS Supports for Emergent Bilingual Learners
lead: How to use these Critical Thinking Online Breakouts with emergent bilingual (EB) students, aligned to the Texas English Language Proficiency Standards (ELPS). The ELPS span four language domains — listening, speaking, reading, and writing — and five proficiency levels. These activities are built to be linguistically accommodated across all seven languages.
goal: 🌱 Start from assets. The ELPS take an asset-based approach: leverage the funds of knowledge, home language, and cultural heritage every student already brings. Cognates and the home-language display build bridges between languages and grow confidence as English develops.
howto: 🧑‍🏫 How to use this page: the four cards summarize the cross-curricular ELPS student expectations for each domain and pair them with concrete moves for these breakouts. The table then shows what each proficiency level looks like and how the activity scaffolds it. Pair this with the UDL supports page and the lesson-plan guide.
accom.p: The ELPS require instruction that is communicated, sequenced, and scaffolded to each student's proficiency level. These breakouts do much of that for you: the 🌐 menu displays every clue and lock in the student's home language beside English; clue cards chunk information into short pieces students can reopen; the word lock accepts spelling variants; and nothing is graded, so students take risks with new language safely. Turn on the home language during a first pass, then invite an English pass for the same puzzle.
dom.listen.exp:
EB students are expected to:
  • distinguish sounds and intonation patterns; respond with gestures, images, orally, or in writing
  • understand content-area vocabulary heard in class
  • follow oral directions with accuracy
  • use context for descriptive language, multiple meanings, and figurative expressions
  • show comprehension by recalling, retelling, responding, or asking for clarification
  • derive meaning from multimedia sources
dom.listen.apply: Try this: read a clue aloud while the home-language text is displayed, then ask students to point to the lock it helps. Let partners restate the clue to each other before choosing an answer. Accept gestures or pointing as a valid response during a first pass.
dom.speak.exp:
EB students are expected to:
  • pronounce newly acquired vocabulary with accuracy
  • speak using content-area and high-frequency vocabulary
  • use a variety of grammatical structures and connecting words
  • use the appropriate register for the setting
  • narrate, describe, or explain with increasing detail
  • restate, ask questions, or respond during interactions
dom.speak.apply: Try this: give sentence stems — “This clue tells me… so the lock is…” Have each pair explain aloud which clue cracked a lock before moving on. Model the target academic word once, then ask students to use it in their explanation.
dom.read.exp:
EB students are expected to:
  • show print awareness and directionality
  • decode words using sound–letter relationships, cognates, and word parts
  • use high-frequency and content-area vocabulary to comprehend text
  • use context for figurative language and multiple meanings
  • use pre-reading strategies — preview, connect to prior knowledge, predict
  • comprehend content-area texts with visual, contextual, and linguistic support
dom.read.apply: Try this: preview the breakout's theme and any word bank before starting (pre-reading). Point out cognates between the home language and English on the clue cards. Let students reopen clues as often as they need — rereading is a strategy, not a failure.
dom.write.exp:
EB students are expected to:
  • represent sounds with letters when writing
  • spell using conventional patterns and rules
  • write using high-frequency and content-area vocabulary
  • use a variety of sentence lengths, types, and connecting words
  • use conventions and grammatical structures
  • write to narrate, describe, explain, respond, or persuade
dom.write.apply: Try this: the word lock is low-stakes writing — it accepts spelling variants, so students focus on the idea. After the breakout, have students write one or two sentences explaining how they solved a lock, using the target vocabulary and a sentence stem.
levels.intro: EB students may be at different levels across the four domains. Match the support to the level; every student can do the cognitively demanding thinking with the right language scaffold.
lvl.pre.look: Silent period; responses are mostly non-verbal.
lvl.pre.scaffold: Display the home language. Accept pointing and gestures. Pair with a bilingual peer. Let the student show the answer, not say it.
lvl.beg.look: One word or short two-to-three-word phrases; repeats keywords.
lvl.beg.scaffold: Provide word banks and sentence stems. Ask yes/no or either/or questions about a clue. Celebrate keyword use.
lvl.int.look: Short phrases and simple sentences; literal comprehension.
lvl.int.scaffold: Ask “which clue and why” questions. Provide extra visual support for abstract or figurative language. Have partners compare reasoning.
lvl.high.look: A variety of sentence types; expresses opinions; asks for clarification.
lvl.high.scaffold: Move to English display with the home language as backup. Ask students to justify and to predict the next lock. Fade the stems.
lvl.adv.look: Engages with little to no linguistic support; uses content-area vocabulary.
lvl.adv.scaffold: Have the student explain their strategy to the group in academic English and mentor a peer. Extend with a transfer question.
disc: ELPS content is summarized and paraphrased for planning support; it is not a substitute for the official standards. Confirm current TEA guidance before adoption.
cite: Standards: Texas Education Agency, English Language Proficiency Standards (19 TAC Chapter 74). Cross-curricular second language acquisition student expectations, listening / speaking / reading / writing.
